questions.problem: A fair seven-sided die with sides labeled with numbers $1$ through $7$ is thrown once. If $X$ is the outcome of the die, what is the variance of $X?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can compute the variance of a discrete random variable $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

First, we need to compute the probability mass function $f(x).$ Here, there are $7$ possible outcomes ($1,2,3,4,5,6,7$) and each outcome has the same probability, so the probability mass function is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ |

Next, we compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4)+5\cdot f(5)+6\cdot f(6)+7\cdot f(7) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{7})+2(\frac{1}{7})+3(\frac{1}{7})+4(\frac{1}{7})+5(\frac{1}{7})+6(\frac{1}{7})+7(\frac{1}{7}) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6)+{7}^{2}\cdot f(7) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{7})+4(\frac{1}{7})+9(\frac{1}{7})+16(\frac{1}{7})+25(\frac{1}{7})+36(\frac{1}{7})+49(\frac{1}{7}) \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =20-{4}^{2} \\  & =20-16 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the ellipsoid $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{9}+(y+2)^{2}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{9}=1$, find its intercepts with the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts, we plug $x=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(0+1)^{2}}{9}+(y+2)^{2}+\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{9}+(y+2)^{2}+\frac{4}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{9}+(y+2)^{2} & =1 \\ (y+2)^{2} & =\frac{4}{9} \\ y+2 & =\pm \frac{2}{3} \\ y & =-2\pm \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $y=-\frac{8}{3}$ and $y=-\frac{4}{3}.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $y$-axis are $(0,-\frac{8}{3},0)$ and $(0,-\frac{4}{3},0).$

questions.problem: Which of the following represents the level curves of $f(x,y)={y}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the range of $f(x,y)$ is $[0,\infty ).$ So, we will consider only $c$-level curves for $c\ge 0.$

The level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equations 

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ {y}^{2} & =c \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{c}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the equations $y=\pm \sqrt{c}$ do not depend on $x.$ So, for a given $c\in [0,\infty ),$ the right-hand side of the equation is constant. As a result, we obtain a family of horizontal lines, as shown below.

questions.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=v-u,\,y=u+v-1.
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]$

II. $det(A)=-2$

III. The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}v-u \\ u+v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u+v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|=1\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1=-2.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $det(A)<0,$ the affine transformation $T$ is not orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+\frac{9}{16}{e}^{6x}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+\frac{9}{16}{e}^{6x}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{9}{16}{e}^{6x}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{3}{4}{e}^{3x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \frac{3}{4}\int {e}^{3x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{4}{e}^{3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\frac{1}{4}{e}^{3x}+4.$

questions.problem: For the differential equation $2{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+xy={x}^{2}-x,$ what is the associated homogeneous equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order inhomogeneous ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is constructed by replacing $f(x)$ with zero:

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=0
$$

Therefore, in our case, the associated homogeneous equation is

$$
2{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+xy=0.
$$

First, we compute ${A}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${A}^{2}=A,$ so $A$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute ${A}^{4}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & ={A}^{2}\cdot {A}^{2} \\  & =A\cdot A \\  & ={A}^{2} \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{A}^{4}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$
